title: Is sleepmaxxing actually helpful?
description:
Researching ways to improve your sleep has been popular for years but now it’s evolved and there’s a whole new genre of social media content called ‘Sleepmaxxing’. It shows ways you can build your perfect night’s sleep, by taking magnesium supplements, using black-out curtains or white noise machines. Experts say the popularity has boomed thanks to the accessibility of smart watches which give users sleep scores. We hear from Ollie, who tracks his sleep and is aiming for the perfect score.

BBC reporter Ashitha Nagesh who’s been reporting on the trend, tells us why some experts advise against multi-layered sleep routines and an obsessive fixation with sleep called orthosomnia.

Plus, sleep expert Sophie Bostock tells us how reliable popular sleep trackers are and what they are really measuring.

summaryZh: 本集 BBC 節目《What in the World》探討社群媒體上熱門的「睡眠極大化」趨勢，以及利用智慧裝置與追蹤器優化睡眠是否真的有效。 BBC 記者 Ashitha Nagesh 指出，全球約有 4 億人正在追蹤睡眠數據，但過度追求高分可能引發名為「完美睡眠症」（ orthosomnia ）的焦慮感，且研究顯示光是看到假給的低睡眠分數，就會讓人在隔天的認知測試中表現變差。節目採訪了記錄自身睡眠數據長達 140 天的創作者 Olly ，並由睡眠專家 Sophie Bostock 分析穿戴式裝置的限制：雖然測量睡眠時間的準確度可達 90% ，但由於裝置無法偵測腦波，對深層或快速動眼期等睡眠階段的判斷準確度僅約 50% 至 80% 。專家建議大眾回歸直覺且良好的睡眠衛生習慣，而非過度焦慮於螢幕上的數字。
summaryEn: This episode of What in the World explores 'sleepmaxxing'—a viral social media trend where people use smart trackers, supplements, and routine tweaks to optimize their sleep and chase high sleep scores. BBC reporter Ashitha Nagesh highlights that while around 400 million people track their sleep, overanalyzing data can cause anxiety and lead to 'orthosomnia' (an obsession with perfect sleep), with research showing that even fake low scores can mentally impair next-day performance. Content creator Olly shares his 140-day journey tracking sleep scores, while sleep expert Sophie Bostock cautions that smartwatches are only 50–80% accurate for sleep stages because they measure movement and heart rate rather than brainwaves. Experts advise focusing on simple, intuitive sleep hygiene instead of stressing over numbers on a screen.
